## 8. Does a worse past change the significance of present relief?

The next test concerns **retained lived history → the ethical significance of an available present transformation**. Including the past in G does not yet decide whether it changes the priority of a later benefit. The proposed comparison applies an established temporal-priority dispute to this generative account; it is not a new discovery in moral philosophy. The [primary reading record](WHOLE-PROCESS-REALIZATION-SOURCES.md#8-past-adversity-and-present-priority) distinguishes the relevant antecedents and their scopes.

### Identify the whole relation before selecting a score

Two continuing participants now undergo comparably severe, unwanted episodes. Relief available now would have matched effects on felt intensity and duration, with matched efficacy, access, costs and foreseeable later consequences. Only one can receive that relief in the present round. Their ages, elapsed lifespans and remaining-life prospects are also matched. Both have received genuine reciprocal care; neither has an unequal prior allocation, undertaking, liability or desert claim concerning this opportunity.

One participant has endured substantially more past adversity; those episodes have ended. The comparison excludes residual differences that would make the present intervention more effective, remove a larger current burden or restore different future opportunities. It does not erase all causal traces: records and knowledge must identify the past accurately. The history is fixed under both available actions. These are demanding conceptual controls, not an empirical claim that all can be matched in practice.

Do not stipulate equal *complete welfare gains* or equal *moral strength*. Those are among the contested conclusions. The stipulated equality concerns independently specified relief and its causal effects. A relational account might argue that the same local relief benefits a whole life differently; another might grant equal benefit but attach different moral importance to it.

The participants are continuities formed within the unfolding, not primitive owners from which a whole is assembled. Identifying which present continuity underwent the earlier adversity is necessary for the proposed historical ground. This requires an account of continuity; it requires neither an unchanging ego nor that every meaningful relation be confined to one individual. Renaming both participants while carrying their histories and relations with them changes no relevant fact. Both competing appraisals can satisfy that invariance.

### An affirmative reason and a substantive rival

The positive lifetime-sensitive proposal is that directing the available good toward the worse lived history can partly redress its disadvantage. Its point concerns how the continuing life goes, rather than a return to whoever supplies relief. The earlier suffering is neither undone nor reclassified as good. A later benefit can improve that life's history without erasing what occurred, and without being payment earned by suffering. This is the proposed ethical relation, not something established by naming the response compensation.

The strongest rival need not deny any of those past experiences, their badness, or the moral significance of either present relief. It may retain the past as a fixed adverse contribution common to both available whole histories, while denying that it changes the comparative force of the present claims under these matched conditions. On that account, the relevant current claims may be equal. Other accounts can combine present severity with lifetime disadvantage instead of making either exclusive.

Thus the dispute is not complete representation versus forgetting the past. It concerns whether the past changes the evaluative contribution of what happens next. Recognizing a genuine historical difference does not establish that it should influence every present choice; recognizing equal local effects does not establish that the full histories have equal significance. Each position owes an account of the relevance it asserts or denies.

### A small diagnostic makes the extra structure explicit

For this illustration only, admit a positive cardinal lifetime-welfare scale and an equal one-unit benefit. Suppose the relevant lifetime outcomes would be A = (2, 4) if relief goes to the historically worse-off participant, and B = (1, 5) if it goes to the other. These numbers are not measurements of the conceptual case or new premises of the generative foundation.

An additive whole-history appraisal gives both outcomes 6. A distinct appraisal sums the square roots of the two lifetime levels:

\[
\sqrt{2}+2 > 1+\sqrt{5}.
\]

Indeed, \(\sqrt{2}+1>\sqrt{5}\), since squaring the positive sides reduces this to \(\sqrt{2}>1\). The second appraisal therefore favors A. Applying any single function to the already equal aggregate 6 would leave the tie intact. The changed ordering comes from a different evaluative structure, not harmless relabeling of the same total. Common positive affine changes of an admitted interval scale preserve equal increments; a nonlinear transform is not merely another such unit choice. This pair alone also cannot distinguish priority to a worse life from concern about inequality.

Both formulas can include the entire relevant past. They are illustrations of independently motivated evaluative alternatives, not arbitrary switches offered as a refutation of the fuller theory. Choosing the second formula would encode a substantive judgment about histories. Its calculation cannot vindicate that judgment. If cardinal comparison is unwarranted, retain the qualitative dispute instead.

Temporal integration does not decide between them. A history-dependent rate or prefix increment can express an already justified history-sensitive appraisal. A temporally additive account can instead retain past adversity while letting its fixed contribution cancel in the present comparison. The representation must follow the defended account of good, rather than settle the question through an unnoticed separability assumption.

### What changes the account, and what remains of the minimum

If earlier adversity causes a larger present burden or different benefits from relief, an account focused on prospective effects can already recognize that difference. If responsibility or a valid undertaking supplies a reparative claim, it introduces another ground. These variants help identify why a judgment changes, but do not decide the controlled historical-priority question. If the alleged continuity or past condition is misidentified, this application fails. A defended argument that lifetime disadvantage modifies benefit or priority would substantively enrich G; a stronger account of present claims could restrict that proposal.

The original minimum retains a positive relief-ground concerning each participant under its defended conditions. Neither available allocation is the earlier no-countervailing-loss improvement: a real burden remains unmet either way. The current disagreement therefore neither refutes that minimum nor closes its grounding. Nor does unresolved priority prove a tie or authorize a lottery by default. Such a procedure needs a separate justification.

The advance is a precise test of ethical content beyond history inclusion. The next derivation must justify how the identified continuity and its lived past bear on present benefit or priority, including limits when the current burdens differ. The whole cannot be reduced to its initiator's return, but that correction alone does not choose a lifetime-weighting rule. No ethical axiom, Lean theorem or completed universal necessity claim is added here.

## 8. Past adversity and present priority

6 October 2026. Root's selected primary readings for [the whole-history comparison](FUTURE-GOOD-INTEGRAL.md#8-does-a-worse-past-change-the-significance-of-present-relief). Link-only provenance: browser-extracted text was read; no original source bytes were imported or source-file hashes claimed. These are philosophical comparisons, not empirical tests of the normative verdict. The project's conceptual case does not adopt a QALY scale or identify disability itself with suffering.

**Dennis McKerlie, “Priority and Time,” Canadian Journal of Philosophy 27(3), 287–309 (1997), [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1080/00455091.1997.10715953).** Read the publisher's [opening extract and notes 4–9](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/canadian-journal-of-philosophy/article/abs/priority-and-time/774CEC357E036AC6681E8F526DD0D141); not the full paper. The website's 2020 online date is not the original publication year. The extract distinguishes benefit size from moral importance; the notes distinguish lifetime and time-specific priority. Note 9 questions whether moral concern for unity of a life depends on personal identity being an additional fact beyond psychological relations. This supports examining generated continuity without treating either its ethical weight or a permanent owner as established.

**Trygve Ottersen, “Lifetime QALY prioritarianism in priority setting,” Journal of Medical Ethics 39(3), 175–180 (2013), [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1136/medethics-2012-100740).** The publisher open returned an access error. Read the [public article-text reproduction](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/233830273_Lifetime_QALY_prioritarianism_in_priority_setting): selected past-quality discussion, the full extracted “Exclusion of past health” section, and conclusions (printed pp. 178–179, browser extraction chiefly lines 802–1236). Figures, complete earlier sections and cited works were not independently read. Ottersen defends lifetime-sensitive priority, considers equal intense present pain, and varies past quality, age and future prospects. He retains both benefit and worse-off principles while leaving their weighting unsettled. This is a primary antecedent for our test, not proof of its verdict or our broader foundation; its individual-centered premises are not silently imported.

**Lars Sandman and Niklas Juth, “Severity and Temporality in Healthcare Priority Setting – A Case for A Condition-specific Affectable Time-neutral Approach” (2024), [publisher full text and DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10728-024-00493-z).** Read abstract and selected publisher-text sections on currency, temporal perspectives, condition trajectories, examples 2–4, short extreme conditions and conclusion (extraction lines 83–146 and 216–249, with additional find excerpts). No complete article, supplementary or cited empirical-study reading is claimed. Their normative target is condition-level severity as a modifier of acceptable cost-effectiveness. They can acknowledge an individual-life intuition while excluding an unaffected interval from that specific modifier. They therefore do not supply a blanket denial of historical relevance or our exact equal-claims rival.

**Our use:** distinguish history-sensitive patient benefit, moral priority and adequacy of a representation. Neither a source's endorsement, majority intuition nor choosing a concave expression establishes their ethical ground. The [institutional comparator](WHOLE-HISTORY-INSTITUTIONAL-COMPARATOR.md) supplies a separate causal interface: continued intervention and changes in outcome definitions must remain visible when estimating the histories to be appraised. It does not adjudicate the priority dispute.

## 8. Continuation: fixed past adversity and present priority

The [new comparison](FUTURE-GOOD-INTEGRAL.md#8-does-a-worse-past-change-the-significance-of-present-relief) addresses ethical content of the whole-history appraisal. Both contributors identified it as more discriminating than repeating a participation mechanism or asserting a fair-surplus benchmark without grounding it. Their bounded repository search found related cumulative-burden and fair-allocation work, but no equivalent controlled test. The source search then identified primary antecedents; this is new integration in the project, not a claim of philosophical novelty.

Review requires matching local felt relief and independent causal effects, ages and prospects, while leaving complete welfare and moral importance open. The past can retain evidential traces without producing an unacknowledged difference in present benefit. Generated continuity need not be an enduring ego, but identifying that continuity does not establish lifetime priority. Both rivals can preserve all past events and be invariant under consistent renaming. The qualitative comparison must survive before a numerical representation is used.

The mathematical illustration distinguishes transforming each admitted lifetime level from transforming an already equal total. It adds evaluative structure rather than changing units, and cannot isolate prioritarianism from equality concern by itself. No-loss dominance remains valid at its previous scope; the scarcity case falls outside its antecedent. An unresolved ranking supplies neither equality nor automatic lottery permission.

The [primary reading limits](WHOLE-PROCESS-REALIZATION-SOURCES.md#8-past-adversity-and-present-priority) are part of the result. Argument reviewers did not independently inspect the primary texts. Sandman–Juth's condition-level account must not be recruited as a universal interpersonal rival. The supporting [GoBifo comparison](WHOLE-HISTORY-INSTITUTIONAL-COMPARATOR.md) constrains exposure and measurement histories, not ethical priority; its two publications concern the same intervention, with later treatment and changed indicators explicitly retained.

This round adds a discriminating ethical test and a hand-worked representation diagnostic. It does not establish either disputed priority rule, add a Lean premise, or complete the universal minimum. [Owned edits](HISTORY-PRIORITY-EDITS.json) and [verification](HISTORY-PRIORITY-CHECKS.json) concern the documented integration and retained formal files, not ethical truth.

### When a fixed past changes present significance

The [historical-priority comparison](../../../_process/research/2026-10-05-generative-foundation-review/root-foundation/FUTURE-GOOD-INTEGRAL.md#8-does-a-worse-past-change-the-significance-of-present-relief) tests more than whether G retains past events. Two formed continuities have matched current burdens, available relief, ages and future prospects, but one has endured substantially greater past adversity. A lifetime-sensitive appraisal may give relief there greater significance. A rival may preserve all of that past while denying greater priority under the matched conditions. Neither requires a privileged initiator or a primitive enduring owner.

The question is whether that history changes the good realized by relief or its moral importance. Those claims cannot be obtained by stipulating equal complete welfare gains, deleting the past, or choosing a nonlinear score. The integral can express either defended appraisal; it does not settle between them. Both participants retain their proposed relief-ground, while scarcity leaves a conflict outside the earlier no-countervailing-loss test. Unresolved priority proves neither a tie nor permission to use a lottery. The remaining derivation must justify the temporal relation's ethical significance and its limits.

A separate [longitudinal empirical comparison](../../../_process/research/2026-10-05-generative-foundation-review/root-foundation/WHOLE-HISTORY-INSTITUTIONAL-COMPARATOR.md) constrains which histories are being evaluated: the actual intervention lineage and outcome definitions must be retained. It supplies no ethical ordering.
